**Préliminaires.** On admet uniquement les propriétés élémentaires de $\mathbb{Z}$ : c'est un anneau commutatif, il est ordonné, toute partie non vide de $\mathbb{N}^{*}$ possède un plus petit élément (bon ordre), et l'on y dispose de la division euclidienne : pour $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ et $q\in\mathbb{N}^{*}$, il existe $k,s\in\mathbb{Z}$ avec $m=kq+s$ et $0\le s<q$.

---

**Lemme 1 (sous-groupes de $\mathbb{Z}$).** Soit $H$ un sous-groupe de $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ non réduit à $\{0\}$. Alors $H=q\mathbb{Z}$, où $q$ est le plus petit élément de $H\cap\mathbb{N}^{*}$.

*Démonstration.* Comme $H\neq\{0\}$, il contient un élément $h\neq 0$, donc aussi $-h$ ; l'un des deux est $>0$, donc $H\cap\mathbb{N}^{*}\neq\varnothing$ et admet un plus petit élément $q$ par bon ordre. Comme $H$ est un sous-groupe contenant $q$, il contient $q\mathbb{Z}$. Réciproquement, soit $m\in H$ ; écrivons $m=kq+s$ avec $0\le s<q$. Alors $s=m-kq\in H$ ; si $s>0$, cela contredit la minimalité de $q$. Donc $s=0$ et $m\in q\mathbb{Z}$. $\square$

**Lemme 2 (Bézout).** Soient $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ non tous deux nuls. Posons $I=\{ua+vb : u,v\in\mathbb{Z}\}$. Alors $I=d\mathbb{Z}$ où $d$ est le plus petit élément de $I\cap\mathbb{N}^{*}$ ; de plus $d$ divise $a$ et $b$, tout diviseur commun de $a$ et $b$ divise $d$, et il existe $u,v\in\mathbb{Z}$ tels que $d=ua+vb$. On note $d=\mathrm{pgcd}(a,b)$.

*Démonstration.* $I$ est visiblement un sous-groupe de $\mathbb{Z}$, non nul car $a=1\cdot a+0\cdot b\in I$ et $b\in I$ et l'un des deux est non nul. Le Lemme 1 donne $I=d\mathbb{Z}$ avec $d=\min(I\cap\mathbb{N}^*)$, et $d\in I$ s'écrit donc $d=ua+vb$. Comme $a,b\in I=d\mathbb{Z}$, $d$ divise $a$ et $b$. Enfin si $c$ divise $a$ et $b$, il divise $ua+vb=d$. $\square$

**Lemme 3.** Soient $t,q\in\mathbb{Z}$ non tous deux nuls avec $\mathrm{pgcd}(t,q)=1$, et soit $k\in\mathbb{N}^{*}$. Alors $\mathrm{pgcd}(t^{k},q)=1$.

*Démonstration.* Par le Lemme 2 il existe $u,v\in\mathbb{Z}$ avec $ut+vq=1$. En élevant à la puissance $k$ et en développant par la formule du binôme, tous les termes contenant au moins un facteur $vq$ sont multiples de $q$ ; il vient
$$1=(ut+vq)^{k}=u^{k}t^{k}+q\,w \qquad\text{pour un certain } w\in\mathbb{Z}.$$
Donc $1$ appartient à l'ensemble $\{u't^{k}+v'q\}=\mathrm{pgcd}(t^k,q)\mathbb{Z}$, d'où $\mathrm{pgcd}(t^{k},q)$ divise $1$, c'est-à-dire vaut $1$. $\square$

---

**Théorème (intégralité des racines rationnelles d'un polynôme unitaire à coefficients entiers).**
Soient $n\ge 1$ et $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}\in\mathbb{Z}$. Si $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ vérifie
$$r^{n}+a_{n-1}r^{n-1}+\dots+a_{1}r+a_{0}=0,$$
alors $r\in\mathbb{Z}$.

*Démonstration.* Si $r=0$, c'est clair. Supposons $r\neq 0$ et posons
$$D=\{m\in\mathbb{Z} : mr\in\mathbb{Z}\}.$$
$D$ est un sous-groupe de $\mathbb{Z}$ : $0\in D$, et si $m,m'\in D$ alors $(m-m')r=mr-m'r\in\mathbb{Z}$. Il est non nul : en écrivant $r=a/b$ avec $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, $b\in\mathbb{N}^{*}$, on a $b\in D$. Par le Lemme 1, $D=q\mathbb{Z}$ où $q=\min(D\cap\mathbb{N}^{*})$ ; posons $t=qr\in\mathbb{Z}$, de sorte que $r=t/q$ et $t\neq 0$.

*(i) $\mathrm{pgcd}(t,q)=1$.* Soit $d=\mathrm{pgcd}(t,q)\ge 1$. Les entiers $t/d$ et $q/d$ sont entiers, et $(q/d)\,r=t/d\in\mathbb{Z}$, donc $q/d\in D\cap\mathbb{N}^{*}$. Par minimalité de $q$, $q/d\ge q$, donc $d\le 1$, donc $d=1$.

*(ii) $q$ divise $t^{n}$.* Multiplions l'équation $r^{n}+a_{n-1}r^{n-1}+\dots+a_{0}=0$ par $q^{n}$. Comme $q^{n}r^{i}=q^{\,n-i}t^{i}$ pour $0\le i\le n$, on obtient
$$t^{n}+a_{n-1}\,q\,t^{n-1}+a_{n-2}\,q^{2}t^{n-2}+\dots+a_{1}q^{n-1}t+a_{0}q^{n}=0,$$
c'est-à-dire
$$t^{n}=-q\left(a_{n-1}t^{n-1}+a_{n-2}\,q\,t^{n-2}+\dots+a_{1}q^{n-2}t+a_{0}q^{n-1}\right),$$
où la parenthèse est un entier. Donc $q\mid t^{n}$.

*(iii) Conclusion.* Par (i) et le Lemme 3, $\mathrm{pgcd}(t^{n},q)=1$. Or $q$ divise $t^{n}$ et $q$ divise $q$, donc $q$ divise $\mathrm{pgcd}(t^{n},q)=1$ (Lemme 2), d'où $q=1$. Ainsi $r=t\in\mathbb{Z}$. $\square$

---

**Corollaire : aucun nombre rationnel n'a pour carré $2$.**

*Démonstration.* Supposons qu'il existe $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ avec $r^{2}=2$. Alors $r$ est racine du polynôme unitaire à coefficients entiers $X^{2}-2$, c'est-à-dire
$$r^{2}+0\cdot r+(-2)=0 .$$
Le théorème (appliqué avec $n=2$, $a_{1}=0$, $a_{0}=-2$) donne $r\in\mathbb{Z}$. Posons $t=|r|\in\mathbb{N}$, de sorte que $t^{2}=2$. Or :

- si $t\le 1$, alors $t^{2}\le t\cdot 1\le 1<2$ ;
- si $t\ge 2$, alors $t^{2}\ge 2t\ge 4>2$.

Ces deux cas épuisent $\mathbb{N}$ et sont tous deux incompatibles avec $t^{2}=2$. Contradiction. Il n'existe donc aucun nombre rationnel dont le carré vaut $2$. $\blacksquare$

proof:
## Setup: what we must show, and how we will translate it into geometry

We want to prove the following statement.

> **Theorem.** There is no rational number $r$ with $r^2 = 2$.

The strategy is one of the oldest in mathematics: we suppose such a number exists, translate that supposition into a statement about a *square* — a genuine geometric square, with a side and a diagonal measured in whole units — and then perform a physical operation on that square (a fold) which produces a *smaller* square of the same kind. Since the whole numbers cannot decrease forever, this is absurd. The technical name for this pattern is *descent*: from one solution we manufacture a strictly smaller one, and since there is a least solution, no solution can exist at all.

Let us begin with the translation from arithmetic to geometry.

Suppose, for contradiction, that some rational number $r$ satisfies $r^2 = 2$. Note that $r \neq 0$ (since $0^2 = 0 \ne 2$), and that $(-r)^2 = r^2 = 2$ as well, so by replacing $r$ with $-r$ if necessary we may assume $r > 0$. Being a positive rational, $r$ can be written as a quotient $r = p/q$ of two **positive integers** $p$ and $q$. Squaring and clearing the denominator, the equation $r^2 = 2$ becomes
$$p^2 = 2q^2 = q^2 + q^2 .$$

Read that last equation with the Pythagorean theorem in mind. It says: *a right triangle whose two legs both have length $q$ has hypotenuse of length exactly $p$.* Such a triangle — a right triangle with two equal legs — is precisely half of a square, cut along a diagonal. Its legs are two sides of the square and its hypotenuse is the diagonal. Let us give it a name.

> **Definition.** Call a triangle a *half-square triangle* if it has a right angle and the two legs adjacent to that right angle are equal. Equivalently, it is a square cut in half along a diagonal; its hypotenuse is that diagonal.

So the assumption that $\sqrt2$ is rational has been converted into the following geometric assertion:

> $(\ast)$ There exists a half-square triangle whose two legs have integer length $q$ and whose hypotenuse has integer length $p$.

Conversely — and we will need this direction in a moment — if we ever produce a half-square triangle whose legs and hypotenuse are all integers, say legs of length $b$ and hypotenuse of length $c$, then the Pythagorean theorem gives $c^2 = b^2 + b^2 = 2b^2$, i.e. $(c/b)^2 = 2$, another rational number whose square is $2$. Thus $(\ast)$ and the Theorem's negation are two ways of saying the same thing. Our task is now to show that $(\ast)$ is impossible.

## Choosing the smallest such triangle

Here is where the descent gets its foothold. Consider the set
$$S = \{\, q \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} : \text{there is a positive integer } p \text{ with } p^2 = 2q^2 \,\},$$
that is, the set of possible *leg lengths* of an integer half-square triangle. By assumption $(\ast)$, the set $S$ is not empty. $$p^2 = 2q^2 .$$

$$CA = CB = q, \qquad \text{hypotenuse } AB = p .$$
Because the two legs are equal, the two base angles are equal, and since the angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ$ we get
$$\angle A = \angle B = 45^\circ, \qquad \angle C = 90^\circ .$$

* Since $p^2 = 2q^2 > q^2$, we get $p > q$. (The diagonal of a square is longer than its side — as it must be, being the hypotenuse.)
* Since $p^2 = 2q^2 < 4q^2 = (2q)^2$, we get $p < 2q$. (The diagonal is shorter than two sides — the triangle inequality, in effect.)

So $q < p < 2q$. Keep these in view; they are what will guarantee that the numbers produced by the fold are *positive*, and that the new triangle is *strictly smaller*.

## The fold

Now take the paper triangle $\triangle ABC$ in your hands. The vertex $A$ is one of the $45^\circ$ corners. Two edges emanate from $A$: the short leg $AC$ (length $q$) and the long hypotenuse $AB$ (length $p$). **Fold the triangle along the crease that bisects the angle at $A$**, so that the hypotenuse $AB$ folds down onto the leg $AC$.

Let us describe this precisely, so that nothing depends on the picture. Let $\ell$ be the bisector of the angle $\angle A$, and let $E$ be the point where $\ell$ meets the opposite side $CB$; since $\ell$ enters the triangle at $A$ and stays inside the angle, it does cross the opposite side, and $E$ lies strictly between $C$ and $B$. Folding along $\ell$ is exactly *reflection in the line $\ell$*. Reflection is a rigid motion: it preserves all lengths and all angles. And by the defining property of an angle bisector, reflection in $\ell$ interchanges the two rays of the angle at $A$: it carries the ray $AC$ onto the ray $AB$ and vice versa.

Follow the three vertices and the crease point:

* $A$ lies on $\ell$, so $A$ stays put.
* $E$ lies on $\ell$, so $E$ stays put.
* $C$ is carried to some point $D$ on the ray $AB$, at the same distance from $A$ as $C$ was; that is, $AD = AC = q$. Since $q < p = AB$, the point $D$ lies **strictly between $A$ and $B$**: the folded leg lands *inside* the hypotenuse.

This is the fold promised in the outline: after folding, the hypotenuse-side of the paper lies along the leg $AC$, and the crease is $AE$. What interests us is the part of the triangle that is *not* covered by the folded flap: the little triangle $\triangle BDE$ near the corner $B$. We now show that it is itself a half-square triangle with integer sides.

**The little triangle has a right angle at $D$.** The reflection carries the segment $CE$ to the segment $DE$ (because $C \mapsto D$ and $E \mapsto E$), and reflections preserve angles; hence
$$\angle ADE = \angle ACE = \angle ACB = 90^\circ .$$
Since $D$ lies between $A$ and $B$, the angle $\angle BDE$ is the supplement of $\angle ADE$, so $\angle BDE = 90^\circ$ as well. Thus $ED \perp AB$.

**The little triangle is a half-square triangle.** In $\triangle BDE$ we have $\angle BDE = 90^\circ$ and $\angle DBE = \angle ABC = 45^\circ$, so the remaining angle is $\angle BED = 45^\circ$. Hence $\triangle BDE$ has two equal angles at $B$ and at $E$, and therefore the sides opposite them are equal:
$$DE = DB .$$
So $\triangle BDE$ is a right triangle whose two legs $DB$ and $DE$ are equal — a half-square triangle, with hypotenuse $BE$. Geometrically: the flap we folded down was itself half of a square, and what remained had to be half of a square too, because the $45^\circ$ angle at $B$ was untouched by the fold and the crease created a fresh right angle at $D$.

**Its sides are integers.** Compute the three relevant lengths, using only the equalities already established and the fact that $D$ lies between $A$ and $B$, and $E$ between $C$ and $B$:

* Leg: $\;DB = AB - AD = p - q$, and this is a *positive* integer because $p > q$.
* Other leg: $\;DE = DB = p - q$, the same positive integer.
* Hypotenuse: reflection gives $CE = DE = p - q$, hence
$$BE = CB - CE = q - (p-q) = 2q - p,$$
which is a *positive* integer because $p < 2q$.

So $\triangle BDE$ is a half-square triangle whose legs have integer length $p - q$ and whose hypotenuse has integer length $2q - p$. By the Pythagorean theorem applied to it,
$$(2q-p)^2 = 2\,(p-q)^2 .$$

## Verifying the identity independently

Because the whole argument rests on this new equation, it is worth checking it by pure algebra as well, so that no unexamined feature of the diagram can be blamed. Starting from $p^2 = 2q^2$:
$$(2q-p)^2 - 2(p-q)^2 = \bigl(4q^2 - 4pq + p^2\bigr) - \bigl(2p^2 - 4pq + 2q^2\bigr) = 2q^2 - p^2 = 0 .$$
So indeed $(2q-p)^2 = 2(p-q)^2$, exactly as the fold predicted. (This is the arithmetic shadow of the fold: it sends the pair $(p,q)$ to the pair $(2q - p,\; p - q)$.)

## The contradiction

Set
$$q' = p - q, \qquad p' = 2q - p .$$
We have shown:

1. $q'$ and $p'$ are positive integers (using $q < p < 2q$);
2. $p'^2 = 2q'^2$.

By (1) and (2), $q'$ belongs to the set $S$ of admissible leg lengths. But
$$q' = p - q < 2q - q = q,$$
again because $p < 2q$. So $q'$ is an element of $S$ strictly smaller than $q$ — contradicting the choice of $q$ as the *least* element of $S$.

In geometric language: the fold takes an integer half-square triangle and produces a strictly smaller integer half-square triangle. Repeating the fold would produce an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers $q > q' > q'' > \cdots$, which is impossible. Either way, the assumption that $S$ is nonempty is untenable.

Therefore no half-square triangle has all of its sides of integer length; that is, statement $(\ast)$ is false. Since we showed that the existence of a rational $r$ with $r^2 = 2$ forces $(\ast)$, we conclude that no such rational number exists. $\blacksquare$

## A remark on what the fold is really saying

It is worth pausing over the mechanism, because it explains why this proof needs no theory of prime numbers, no notion of even and odd, and no reduction of fractions to lowest terms. The fold uses only the rigidity of reflection and the fact that a $45^\circ$ angle survives folding. What it exploits is a purely geometric self-similarity: *inside every half-square triangle there is a smaller half-square triangle, obtained by folding the hypotenuse onto a leg, and the new side lengths are differences of the old ones.* Differences of whole numbers are whole numbers; so if the original triangle had whole-number sides, so does the new one, forever. An unending descent through the positive integers is impossible, so no such triangle can have whole-number sides at all — the side and the diagonal of a square are *incommensurable*, admitting no common unit of measurement, which is precisely the statement that $\sqrt{2}$ is not a ratio of whole numbers.

**Claim.** There is no rational number whose square is 2.

**Proof.**

Suppose, for contradiction, that some rational number has square 2. Writing that rational number as a quotient of positive integers, we get positive integers $a,b$ with

$$a^2 = 2b^2 .$$

By the Pythagorean theorem, this says exactly the following geometric thing:

> There exists an isosceles right triangle whose two legs and whose hypotenuse all have integer length (legs $b$, hypotenuse $a$).

Call such a triangle an *integral half-square*. By the assumption, integral half-squares exist. The set of hypotenuse lengths of integral half-squares is a nonempty set of positive integers, so by the well-ordering principle we may choose an integral half-square

$$\triangle ABC,\qquad \angle C = 90^\circ,\qquad CA = CB = b,\qquad AB = a,$$

whose hypotenuse $a$ is as small as possible. All of $a,b$ are positive integers, and the base angles satisfy $\angle A = \angle B = 45^\circ$.

*Two size facts.* From $a^2 = 2b^2 > b^2$ we get $a > b$. From $a^2 = 2b^2 < 4b^2$ we get $a < 2b$. So

$$b < a < 2b. \tag{$\ast$}$$

**The construction (fold a leg onto the hypotenuse).** Take the leg $BC$ and fold it down onto the hypotenuse, pivoting at $B$: that is, mark on segment $AB$ the point $D$ with

$$BD = BC = b .$$

Since $0 < b < a$ by $(\ast)$, the point $D$ lies strictly between $A$ and $B$. Now, from $D$, raise the perpendicular to $AB$ on the same side as $C$; let $E$ be the point where it meets the leg $AC$.

*Why this perpendicular really does hit the leg $AC$, strictly between $A$ and $C$.* Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Since the triangle is isosceles, $CM \perp AB$, and $BM = a/2$. By $(\ast)$, $BD = b > a/2 = BM$, so $D$ lies strictly between $A$ and $M$. The perpendicular to $AB$ at $D$ is parallel to the perpendicular $MC$ at $M$ and distinct from it, so the ray we raised at $D$ never crosses line $MC$; it stays in the open half-plane bounded by line $MC$ that contains $A$. The triangle is convex and the ray starts at the boundary point $D$ pointing into the interior, so it leaves the triangle through exactly one further boundary point; that point lies on the $A$-side of line $MC$ and is not on $AB$ (a line meets $AB$ only at $D$). Hence it lies on segment $AC$, and it is neither $A$ (the ray starts inside) nor $C$ (which is on the other, parallel line). So $E$ exists and lies strictly between $A$ and $C$.

**Reading off the lengths.**

1. *The folded piece.* Compare triangles $BDE$ and $BCE$. They share the hypotenuse $BE$; each has a right angle ($\angle BDE = 90^\circ$ by construction, and $\angle BCE = 90^\circ$ because $E$ lies on $CA$ and $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$); and $BD = BC$ by construction. By hypotenuse–leg congruence, $\triangle BDE \cong \triangle BCE$. Therefore
$$ED = EC .$$
(This is just the statement that folding along the crease $BE$ carries the leg $BC$ exactly onto the segment $BD$ of the hypotenuse, so the tail $CE$ of the leg lands on the segment $DE$.)

2. *The small triangle.* In triangle $ADE$ we have $\angle ADE = 90^\circ$ and $\angle DAE = \angle A = 45^\circ$, hence $\angle AED = 45^\circ$ and so $ADE$ is again an isosceles right triangle with legs $AD$ and $DE$ and hypotenuse $AE$. Its leg is
$$AD = AB - BD = a - b,$$
and therefore also
$$DE = AD = a-b,\qquad\text{so by (1)}\qquad EC = a-b .$$
Its hypotenuse is
$$AE = AC - EC = b - (a-b) = 2b - a .$$

**The contradiction.** The triangle $ADE$ is an isosceles right triangle whose legs have length $a-b$ and whose hypotenuse has length $2b-a$; both numbers are integers, and both are positive by $(\ast)$ (indeed $E$ lies strictly between $A$ and $C$ and $D$ strictly between $A$ and $B$, so the triangle is genuine). Thus $ADE$ is an integral half-square. But its hypotenuse satisfies

$$2b - a < a \qquad\text{(because } b < a \text{ implies } 2b < 2a\text{)},$$

so it is an integral half-square with hypotenuse strictly smaller than $a$. This contradicts the minimality of $a$.

Hence no integral half-square exists, so there are no positive integers with $a^2 = 2b^2$, i.e. no rational number has square 2. $\blacksquare$

**The picture in one sentence.** Fold one leg of an integer isosceles right triangle onto its hypotenuse; the crease cuts off a strictly smaller isosceles right triangle whose sides are again integers ($a-b$, $a-b$, $2b-a$) — and an endless shrinking of positive integers is impossible.

**Teorema.** No existe ningún número racional $q$ tal que $q^2 = 6$.

*Demostración.* Es consecuencia inmediata del algoritmo de la división: dado $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, existen enteros únicos $k$ y $r$ con $n = 2k + r$ y $0 \le r < 2$; por tanto $r=0$ (y $n$ es par) o $r=1$ (y $n$ es impar), y la unicidad de $r$ garantiza que ambos casos son excluyentes. $\blacksquare$

**Lema 2.** El producto de dos enteros impares es impar.

*Demostración.* Sean $m = 2k+1$ y $n = 2l+1$ con $k,l\in\mathbb{Z}$. Entonces
$$mn = 4kl + 2k + 2l + 1 = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1,$$
que es de la forma $2j+1$ con $j = 2kl+k+l \in \mathbb{Z}$; luego $mn$ es impar. $\blacksquare$

**Lema 3.** Si $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ y $n^2$ es par, entonces $n$ es par.

*Demostración.* Por el Lema 1, si $n$ no fuese par sería impar, y por el Lema 2 (con $m=n$) el producto $n\cdot n = n^2$ sería impar, lo cual contradice, de nuevo por el Lema 1, que $n^2$ sea par. Por tanto $n$ es par. $\blacksquare$

**Demostración del Teorema.**

Supongamos, buscando una contradicción, que existe un número racional $q$ con $q^2 = 6$. Todo racional se escribe como cociente de un entero entre un entero positivo, de modo que existen $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ y $b \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ con $q = \dfrac{a}{b}$. De $q^2 = 6$ se sigue, multiplicando por $b^2 \neq 0$,
$$a^2 = 6b^2 .$$

Consideremos entonces el conjunto
$$S = \{\, b \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} : \text{existe } a \in \mathbb{Z} \text{ tal que } a^2 = 6b^2 \,\}.$$
Por lo anterior, $S \neq \varnothing$. Como $S$ es un subconjunto no vacío de los enteros positivos, el principio de buena ordenación garantiza que $S$ posee un elemento mínimo; llamémoslo $b_0$, y sea $a_0 \in \mathbb{Z}$ tal que
$$a_0^{\,2} = 6\,b_0^{\,2}. \tag{1}$$

**Paso 1: $a_0$ es par.** En efecto, $a_0^{\,2} = 6b_0^{\,2} = 2\,(3b_0^{\,2})$ es par, luego por el Lema 3 el entero $a_0$ es par. Escribamos $a_0 = 2c$ con $c\in\mathbb{Z}$.

**Paso 2: $b_0$ es par.** Sustituyendo $a_0 = 2c$ en (1) obtenemos
$$4c^2 = 6\,b_0^{\,2},$$
y dividiendo entre $2$ (lo que es lícito en $\mathbb{Z}$ pues ambos miembros son múltiplos de $2$):
$$2c^2 = 3\,b_0^{\,2}. \tag{2}$$
Así, $3b_0^{\,2}$ es par. Si $b_0$ fuera impar, entonces por el Lema 2 $b_0^{\,2}=b_0\cdot b_0$ sería impar y, aplicando otra vez el Lema 2 al producto de los impares $3$ y $b_0^{\,2}$, el número $3b_0^{\,2}$ sería impar, contradiciendo el Lema 1. Por consiguiente $b_0$ es par: $b_0 = 2d$ con $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, y $d>0$ porque $b_0>0$.

**Paso 3: contradicción.** Sustituyendo $b_0 = 2d$ en (2):
$$2c^2 = 3\cdot 4d^2 = 12 d^2,$$
y dividiendo entre $2$:
$$c^2 = 6d^2 .$$
Esto muestra que $d \in S$, pues $d$ es un entero positivo y $c$ es un entero que cumple la condición requerida. Pero
$$d = \frac{b_0}{2} < b_0 ,$$
ya que $b_0 > 0$. Tenemos entonces un elemento de $S$ estrictamente menor que el mínimo $b_0$ de $S$, lo cual es absurdo.

La contradicción proviene de suponer la existencia de un racional $q$ con $q^2=6$. Por lo tanto, no existe ningún número racional cuyo cuadrado sea $6$. $\blacksquare$

Suppose, for contradiction, that some $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ satisfies $r^2 = 2$. Write $r = \pm a/b$ with $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$; then $a^2 = 2b^2$. Hence

$$T := \{\, p \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} : \exists\, q \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0},\ p^2 = 2q^2 \,\} \neq \emptyset .$$

By well-ordering let $p = \min T$, and fix $q \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ with

$$p^2 = 2q^2. \tag{1}$$

**Step 1: $q < p < 2q$.** From (1), $p^2 = 2q^2 > q^2$, so $p > q$. Also $p^2 = 2q^2 < 4q^2$, so $p < 2q$. Consequently

$$0 < p - q < q, \qquad 0 < 2q - p < p, \qquad p - q < q. \tag{2}$$

**Step 2: the covering.** In $\mathbb{R}^2$ put

$$S := [0,p]^2, \quad A := [0,q]^2, \quad B := [p-q,p]^2 .$$

By Step 1, $0 < q < p$ and $0 < p-q < p$, so $A, B \subseteq S$; $A$ and $B$ are squares of side $q$ placed in opposite corners of $S$.

*Overlap.* $A \cap B = [p-q,\,q]^2$, a square of side $q-(p-q) = 2q-p > 0$ by (2). Thus

$$\operatorname{area}(A \cap B) = (2q-p)^2. \tag{3}$$

*Complement.* Set
$$C := [q,p] \times [0,p-q], \qquad D := [0,p-q] \times [q,p],$$
squares of side $p-q>0$. Let $(x,y) \in S$ with $(x,y) \notin A^\circ \cup B^\circ$, i.e. ($x \ge q$ or $y \ge q$) and ($x \le p-q$ or $y \le p-q$). Since $p-q < q$ by (2), the cases ($x\ge q$ and $x \le p-q$) and ($y \ge q$ and $y \le p-q$) are impossible; hence either ($x \ge q$ and $y \le p-q$), giving $(x,y) \in C$, or ($y \ge q$ and $x \le p-q$), giving $(x,y) \in D$. Conversely $C, D \subseteq S \setminus (A^\circ \cup B^\circ)$. Also $C \cap D = \emptyset$, since $q > p-q$. Therefore, up to a set of measure zero, $S \setminus (A \cup B) = C \sqcup D$ and

$$\operatorname{area}\big(S \setminus (A\cup B)\big) = 2(p-q)^2. \tag{4}$$

**Step 3: the area identity.** By inclusion–exclusion and (1),

$$\operatorname{area}(A \cup B) = \operatorname{area}(A) + \operatorname{area}(B) - \operatorname{area}(A\cap B) = 2q^2 - \operatorname{area}(A \cap B) = p^2 - \operatorname{area}(A\cap B),$$

while $\operatorname{area}(S) = p^2$. Hence

**Theorem.** There is no $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r^{2} = 2$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{Z}$ denotes the ring of integers and $\mathbb{Q}$ its field of fractions. We give two independent proofs: the first through the theory of irreducibility of polynomials over a unique factorization domain, the second through the theory of quadratic residues and the analytic theory of primes in arithmetic progressions.

---

### Machinery invoked

**Theorem A (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic; Gauss).** $\mathbb{Z}$ is a unique factorization domain: every nonzero non-unit of $\mathbb{Z}$ is a product of primes, uniquely up to order and units. In particular $2$ is a prime element of $\mathbb{Z}$.

**Theorem B (Gauss's Lemma).** Let $R$ be a unique factorization domain with fraction field $K$. The product of primitive polynomials in $R[X]$ is primitive, and consequently a primitive polynomial of $R[X]$ that is irreducible in $R[X]$ remains irreducible in $K[X]$. Equivalently: if $f \in R[X]$ is nonconstant and factors in $K[X]$ as $f = gh$ with $\deg g, \deg h \ge 1$, then $f$ factors in $R[X]$ as $f = g_{1}h_{1}$ with $\deg g_{1} = \deg g$, $\deg h_{1} = \deg h$.

**Theorem C (Eisenstein's Criterion).** Let $R$ be a unique factorization domain with fraction field $K$, let
$$f = a_{n}X^{n} + a_{n-1}X^{n-1} + \dots + a_{0} \in R[X], \qquad n \ge 1,$$
and let $p \in R$ be a prime element such that
$$p \nmid a_{n}, \qquad p \mid a_{i} \ \ (0 \le i \le n-1), \qquad p^{2} \nmid a_{0}.$$
Then $f$ is irreducible as an element of $K[X]$.

**Theorem D (Division Algorithm in $K[X]$, whence the Factor Theorem).** For a field $K$, the ring $K[X]$ is a Euclidean domain with respect to degree; consequently, for $f \in K[X]$ and $r \in K$ we have $f(r) = 0$ if and only if $(X - r) \mid f$ in $K[X]$.

**Theorem E (Degree additivity; units of $K[X]$).** For a field $K$, $K[X]$ is an integral domain and $\deg(gh) = \deg g + \deg h$ for nonzero $g,h$. Hence the units of $K[X]$ are exactly the nonzero constants, and a polynomial of degree $1$ is a non-unit.

**Theorem F (Euler's Criterion and multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol; Euler, Legendre).** For an odd prime $p$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $p \nmid a$, the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{a}{p}\right) \in \{\pm 1\}$ satisfies $\left(\frac{a}{p}\right) \equiv a^{(p-1)/2} \pmod p$, and $\left(\frac{a}{p}\right) = 1$ if and only if $a$ is a square modulo $p$. It is multiplicative in $a$.

**Theorem G (Second Supplementary Law of Quadratic Reciprocity; Gauss).** For every odd prime $p$,
$$\left(\frac{2}{p}\right) = (-1)^{(p^{2}-1)/8},$$
so that $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right) = 1$ iff $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 8$ and $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right) = -1$ iff $p \equiv \pm 3 \pmod 8$.

**Theorem H (Dirichlet's Theorem on Primes in Arithmetic Progressions).** If $a, m$ are coprime positive integers, then there are infinitely many primes $p \equiv a \pmod m$; indeed $\sum_{p \equiv a (m)} p^{-s}$ diverges as $s \to 1^{+}$.

---

### First proof (Eisenstein–Gauss)

Consider $f = X^{2} - 2 \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$, so $a_{2} = 1$, $a_{1} = 0$, $a_{0} = -2$.

By Theorem A, $\mathbb{Z}$ is a unique factorization domain and $p = 2$ is a prime element of $\mathbb{Z}$. We check the hypotheses of Eisenstein's Criterion (Theorem C) with $R = \mathbb{Z}$, $K = \mathbb{Q}$, $p = 2$, $n = 2$:

* $p \nmid a_{2}$: indeed $2 \nmid 1$, since $1$ is a unit and $2$ is not.
* $p \mid a_{1}$ and $p \mid a_{0}$: indeed $2 \mid 0$ and $2 \mid -2$.
* $p^{2} \nmid a_{0}$: indeed $4 \nmid -2$, since $-2 = 4k$ would give $2k \cdot 2 = -2$, hence $-1 = 2k$ contradicting that $2$ is not a unit (equivalently, contradicting uniqueness of factorization in Theorem A).

Hence, by Theorem C (whose proof rests on Theorem B, Gauss's Lemma), $f = X^{2} - 2$ is **irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[X]$**.

Now suppose, for contradiction, that some $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ satisfies $r^{2} = 2$. Then $f(r) = r^{2} - 2 = 0$, so by the Factor Theorem (Theorem D) there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ with
$$X^{2} - 2 = (X - r)\, q(X).$$
By degree additivity (Theorem E), $\deg q = 2 - 1 = 1$. Thus $f$ is a product of two polynomials of degree $1$, each of which is a non-unit of $\mathbb{Q}[X]$ by Theorem E. Moreover $f$ itself is not a unit (its degree is $2 \neq 0$) and is nonzero. Therefore $f$ is a nonzero non-unit expressed as a product of two non-units, i.e. $f$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[X]$ — contradicting the irreducibility established above.

(Equivalently, in the language of field theory: by irreducibility, $X^{2}-2$ is the minimal polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$ of any of its roots $\alpha$ in an algebraic closure, so $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 2$; if $\alpha$ were rational then $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) = \mathbb{Q}$ and the multiplicativity of degrees in towers would force $2 = [\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 1$, absurd.)

Hence no rational number has square $2$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

---

### Second proof (Quadratic Reciprocity and Dirichlet)

Suppose for contradiction that $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ satisfies $r^{2} = 2$, and write $r = a/b$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$, $b \neq 0$. Then
$$a^{2} = 2b^{2}. \tag{$*$}$$

Since $3$ and $8$ are coprime, Dirichlet's Theorem (Theorem H) provides infinitely many primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod 8$. As $2b^{2} \neq 0$ has only finitely many prime divisors, we may choose such a prime $p$ with $p \nmid 2b$; note $p$ is odd (indeed $p \equiv 3 \bmod 8$ forces $p$ odd, and $p \ne 3$ may also be arranged, though it is not needed).

Because $p \nmid b$, the class of $b$ is invertible in the field $\mathbb{F}_{p} = \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$; let $\bar b^{-1}$ denote its inverse. Reducing $(*)$ modulo $p$ gives
$$\bar a^{2} = 2\,\bar b^{2}, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad 2 = \left(\bar a \, \bar b^{-1}\right)^{2} \ \text{ in } \mathbb{F}_{p}.$$
Also $p \nmid 2$, so $2 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$ and thus $\bar a\bar b^{-1} \neq 0$. Therefore $2$ is a nonzero square modulo $p$, and by Euler's Criterion (Theorem F),
$$\left(\frac{2}{p}\right) = 1 .$$
On the other hand, since $p \equiv 3 \pmod 8$, the Second Supplementary Law of Quadratic Reciprocity (Theorem G) gives
$$\left(\frac{2}{p}\right) = (-1)^{(p^{2}-1)/8} = -1 ,$$
because $p^{2} \equiv 9 \pmod{16}$ shows $(p^{2}-1)/8$ is odd. Thus $1 = -1$ in $\{\pm 1\} \subset \mathbb{Z}$, which is false.

This contradiction shows that no rational $r$ satisfies $r^{2} = 2$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

### Remark (the same obstruction, seen from on high)

Both proofs detect a single arithmetic phenomenon: the prime $2$ ramifies in the quadratic field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$. Indeed, in the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{K} = \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{2}]$ one has the factorization of ideals $(2) = (\sqrt2)^{2}$, so by the Dedekind–Kummer theorem the discriminant $d_{K} = 8 \neq 1$; by Minkowski's theorem on discriminants (or simply by the Kronecker–Weber description of $K$ as the quadratic subfield of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{8})$), a number field with $|d_{K}| > 1$ is not $\mathbb{Q}$, so $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$. The second proof above is precisely this statement made explicit, with Dirichlet's theorem and Gauss's reciprocity law supplying the required inert primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod 8$.

**Theorem.** There is no rational number $r$ such that $r^2 = 2$.

**Preliminary conventions.** An integer $n$ is called *even* if $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$, and *odd* if $n = 2k+1$ for some integer $k$. A rational number is a number of the form $p/q$ where $p$ and $q$ are integers and $q \neq 0$. We use the following standard facts about the integers: they are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication; the usual order properties hold; every integer is either even or odd; and the well-ordering principle holds, i.e. every nonempty set of positive integers has a least element.

**Lemma 1.** No integer is both even and odd.

*Proof.* Suppose $n$ were both, say $n = 2k$ and $n = 2j+1$ with $k, j$ integers. Then $2k = 2j + 1$, so $2(k - j) = 1$. Put $c = k - j$, an integer with $2c = 1$. If $c \le 0$ then $2c \le 0 < 1$; if $c \ge 1$ then $2c \ge 2 > 1$. Since every integer satisfies $c \le 0$ or $c \ge 1$, both cases are impossible, and we have a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.** If $n$ is an integer and $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even.

*Proof.* Suppose $n$ is not even. Then $n$ is odd, say $n = 2k+1$ with $k$ an integer. Then
$$n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1,$$
and since $2k^2 + 2k$ is an integer, $n^2$ is odd. But $n^2$ is even by hypothesis, contradicting Lemma 1. Hence $n$ is even. $\blacksquare$

**Proof of the Theorem.** Suppose, for contradiction, that $r$ is a rational number with $r^2 = 2$. Write $r = p/q$ with $p, q$ integers and $q \neq 0$. From $p^2/q^2 = 2$ we get
$$p^2 = 2q^2 .$$
Note $p \neq 0$: if $p = 0$, then $2q^2 = 0$, so $q = 0$, contrary to $q \neq 0$. Put $a = |p|$ and $b = |q|$. Then $a$ and $b$ are positive integers and, since $a^2 = p^2$ and $b^2 = q^2$,
$$a^2 = 2b^2 .$$

Thus the set
$$S = \{\, b \in \mathbb{Z} : b \ge 1 \text{ and } a^2 = 2b^2 \text{ for some integer } a \ge 1 \,\}$$
is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle, $S$ has a least element $b_0$, and there is a positive integer $a_0$ with
$$a_0^2 = 2b_0^2 .$$

Since $a_0^2 = 2b_0^2$ and $b_0^2$ is an integer, $a_0^2$ is even, so by Lemma 2 the integer $a_0$ is even: $a_0 = 2c$ for some integer $c$. Moreover $c \ge 1$, because $2c = a_0 \ge 1$ forces $c > 0$. Substituting,
$$4c^2 = (2c)^2 = a_0^2 = 2b_0^2 ,$$
and dividing by $2$ gives
$$b_0^2 = 2c^2 .$$

This equation shows two things.

First, $c \in S$: indeed $c$ is a positive integer and $b_0$ is a positive integer with $b_0^2 = 2c^2$.

Second, $c < b_0$: from $b_0^2 = 2c^2 = c^2 + c^2 > c^2$ (using $c^2 > 0$, as $c \ge 1$), we get $b_0^2 > c^2$; since $b_0$ and $c$ are positive, $b_0 \le c$ would give $b_0^2 \le c^2$, so we must have $b_0 > c$.

Hence $c$ is an element of $S$ strictly smaller than $b_0$, contradicting the minimality of $b_0$.

Therefore no rational number has square equal to $2$. $\blacksquare$

**Afirmación.** Existe un único número real $x$ tal que $x^3=x+1$, y ese número es irracional.

---

**1. Existencia y unicidad del número real $x$.**

Consideremos la función $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ dada por
$$f(t)=t^3-t-1,$$
que es continua (es un polinomio). Como $f(1)=1-1-1=-1<0$ y $f(2)=8-2-1=5>0$, el teorema del valor intermedio garantiza que existe $x\in(1,2)$ con $f(x)=0$, es decir, $x^3=x+1$. Esto prueba la existencia.

Para la unicidad, veamos primero que toda raíz real de $f$ es mayor que $1$. Escribamos $f(t)=t(t^2-1)-1$.

- Si $t\le -1$, entonces $t<0$ y $t^2-1\ge 0$, luego $t(t^2-1)\le 0$ y por tanto $f(t)\le -1<0$.
- Si $-1\le t\le 1$, entonces $|t|\le 1$ y $|t^2-1|\le 1$, de modo que $|t(t^2-1)|\le 1$; en realidad basta con $t(t^2-1)\le |t|\,|t^2-1|\le 1$, pero necesitamos desigualdad estricta con $1$: si $t(t^2-1)=1$ con $|t|\le 1$, entonces $|t|=1$ y $|t^2-1|=1$, lo cual es imposible pues $|t|=1$ implica $t^2-1=0$. Así $t(t^2-1)<1$ y por tanto $f(t)<0$.

En consecuencia $f(t)<0$ para todo $t\le 1$, y toda raíz real de $f$ cumple $t>1$. Ahora, si $1<a<b$, entonces
$$f(b)-f(a)=(b^3-a^3)-(b-a)=(b-a)\bigl(a^2+ab+b^2-1\bigr)>0,$$
porque $b-a>0$ y $a^2+ab+b^2>1+1+1-1>0$ (de hecho $a^2+ab+b^2>3>1$). Luego $f$ es estrictamente creciente en $(1,\infty)$ y no puede anularse dos veces allí. Como todas las raíces reales están en $(1,\infty)$, la raíz es única. Llamemos $x$ a ese número.

**2. El número $x$ es irracional.**

Razonamos por reducción al absurdo. Supongamos que $x\in\mathbb{Q}$. Entonces $x$ se puede escribir en forma irreducible
$$x=\frac{p}{q},\qquad p\in\mathbb{Z},\ q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0},\ \gcd(p,q)=1 .$$

Sustituyendo en $x^3=x+1$:
$$\frac{p^3}{q^3}=\frac{p}{q}+1 .$$
Multiplicando ambos miembros por $q^3>0$ obtenemos la igualdad entre enteros
$$p^3=p\,q^2+q^3 . \tag{$*$}$$

De $(*)$ se sigue que $q$ divide a $p^3$, ya que $p^3=q\,(p q+q^2)$.

Supongamos que $q>1$. Entonces $q$ tiene un divisor primo $r$. Como $r\mid q$ y $q\mid p^3$, tenemos $r\mid p^3$. Puesto que $r$ es primo, del lema de Euclides se deduce $r\mid p$. Pero entonces $r$ es un divisor común de $p$ y $q$ mayor que $1$, lo que contradice $\gcd(p,q)=1$. Por tanto $q=1$, es decir, $x=p$ es un número entero.

Sustituyendo $q=1$ en $(*)$ (o directamente en la ecuación) queda
$$p^3=p+1,\qquad\text{es decir}\qquad p^3-p=1,$$
o bien
$$p\,(p^2-1)=1 .$$
Así, $p$ es un entero que divide a $1$, luego $p\in\{1,-1\}$. Pero en ambos casos $p^2-1=0$, y entonces $p(p^2-1)=0\neq 1$. Contradicción.

(Alternativamente: por el apartado 1 sabemos que $1<x<2$, y no hay ningún entero estrictamente entre $1$ y $2$, lo que ya contradice que $x$ sea entero.)

Como la suposición $x\in\mathbb{Q}$ conduce a una contradicción, concluimos que
$$x\notin\mathbb{Q},$$
es decir, el único número real que satisface $x^3=x+1$ es irracional. $\blacksquare$

**Idea central (ajena al enunciado).** No usaremos paridad, ni factorización única, ni divisibilidad más allá de lo trivial. Usaremos un principio de naturaleza topológica–geométrica (propio de la *geometría de los números*): un subgrupo aditivo de la recta que además sea cerrado bajo productos y contenga algún elemento estrictamente entre $0$ y $1$ no puede ser **discreto**, porque las potencias de ese elemento se acumulan en $0$; en cambio, si $\sqrt2$ fuera racional, todo el anillo $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$ viviría dentro del retículo discreto $\frac1q\mathbb{Z}$, cuyos elementos no nulos están separados de $0$. La contradicción es entre "hay elementos no nulos arbitrariamente pequeños" y "todos los elementos no nulos miden al menos $1/q$". Todo el argumento se hace dentro de $\mathbb{Q}$, de modo que no se presupone la existencia del número real $\sqrt2$.

---

**Teorema.** No existe $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ tal que $r^2=2$.

**Demostración.** Supongamos, por reducción al absurdo, que existe $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ con $r^{2}=2$. Como $(-r)^2=r^2$, podemos suponer $r>0$ (nótese que $r\neq 0$, pues $0^2=0\neq2$).

*Paso 1: $1<r<2$.*
Si fuera $r\le 1$, entonces, al ser $r>0$, multiplicando $r\le 1$ por $r>0$ obtendríamos $r^{2}\le r\le 1<2$, contra $r^2=2$. Si fuera $r\ge 2$, multiplicando por $r>0$ obtendríamos $r^{2}\ge 2r\ge 4>2$, de nuevo una contradicción. Luego $1<r<2$.

*Paso 2: el conjunto $R=\{a+br:\ a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ es cerrado bajo sumas y productos.*
La cerradura bajo sumas es inmediata. Para los productos, usando $r^{2}=2$:
$$(a+br)(c+dr)=ac+(ad+bc)\,r+bd\,r^{2}=(ac+2bd)+(ad+bc)\,r,$$
y $ac+2bd,\ ad+bc\in\mathbb{Z}$. Así, $R$ es cerrado bajo productos. En particular, si $x\in R$, entonces $x^{n}\in R$ para todo entero $n\ge 1$ (inducción sobre $n$).

*Paso 3: todos los elementos de $R$ tienen denominador acotado.*
Como $r\in\mathbb{Q}$, escribamos $r=p/q$ con $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$, $q\ge 1$ (no hace falta que la fracción sea irreducible). Entonces, para $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$,
$$a+br=a+b\frac{p}{q}=\frac{aq+bp}{q},$$
con $aq+bp\in\mathbb{Z}$. Por tanto $R\subseteq \frac1q\mathbb{Z}$, y en consecuencia:
$$\text{si } x\in R \text{ y } x\neq 0,\quad \text{entonces } |x|\ge \frac{1}{q}, \tag{$\ast$}$$
pues $x=m/q$ con $m\in\mathbb{Z}$, $m\neq0$, luego $|m|\ge1$. (Esta es la *discreción* del retículo $\frac1q\mathbb{Z}$.)

*Paso 4: $R$ contiene potencias positivas arbitrariamente pequeñas.*
Sea $\theta:=r-1$. Por el Paso 1, $0<\theta<1$; y $\theta\in R$ (tomando $a=-1$, $b=1$). Por el Paso 2, $\theta^{n}\in R$ para todo $n\ge1$, y $\theta^{n}>0$ (producto de números positivos), en particular $\theta^n\neq 0$.

Acotemos $\theta^{n}$. Como $0<\theta<1$, el número
$$x:=\frac{1-\theta}{\theta}\in\mathbb{Q}$$
es estrictamente positivo, y se cumple $\theta=\dfrac{1}{1+x}$, pues $1+x=1+\frac{1-\theta}{\theta}=\frac1\theta$.

Probemos la desigualdad de Bernoulli $(1+x)^{n}\ge 1+nx$ para todo entero $n\ge1$, por inducción: para $n=1$ es una igualdad; y si $(1+x)^{n}\ge 1+nx$, entonces, multiplicando por $1+x>0$,
$$(1+x)^{n+1}\ge (1+nx)(1+x)=1+(n+1)x+nx^{2}\ge 1+(n+1)x .$$
Por lo tanto, para todo $n\ge1$,
$$0<\theta^{n}=\frac{1}{(1+x)^{n}}\le\frac{1}{1+nx}. \tag{$\ast\ast$}$$

*Paso 5: elección de $n$ y contradicción.*
Escribamos $x=s/t$ con $s,t$ enteros positivos (posible porque $x\in\mathbb{Q}$, $x>0$). Tomemos $n:=tq\ \ (\ge 1)$. Entonces
$$1+nx=1+tq\cdot\frac{s}{t}=1+qs\ge 1+q>q,$$
ya que $s\ge1$. Combinando con $(\ast\ast)$:
$$0<\theta^{\,n}\le\frac{1}{1+nx}<\frac{1}{q}.$$
Pero $\theta^{n}$ es un elemento **no nulo** de $R$, de modo que $(\ast)$ obliga a $\theta^{n}\ge 1/q$. Hemos obtenido $\theta^{n}<1/q$ y $\theta^{n}\ge1/q$ simultáneamente: contradicción.

Por consiguiente, no existe ningún $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ con $r^{2}=2$. $\blacksquare$

---

**Observación.** El argumento no usó en ningún momento que $p$ y $q$ fueran coprimos, ni el concepto de número par, ni el teorema fundamental de la aritmética: sólo la estructura de anillo de $\mathbb{Z}[r]$ (Paso 2), la discreción de $\frac1q\mathbb{Z}$ (Paso 3) y el hecho de que las potencias de un elemento de $(0,1)$ se hacen tan pequeñas como se quiera (Paso 4). Es, en miniatura, el mismo mecanismo de las demostraciones de irracionalidad de tipo Liouville y de la clasificación de los subgrupos de $\mathbb{R}$ en discretos o densos.

Write a complete, correct, self-contained proof that there is no rational number whose square is 2.

Take the smallest such p, lay the two smaller squares into opposite corners of the larger one, and observe that the doubly covered square in the middle has the same area as the two uncovered corner squares -- a strictly smaller instance, contradicting minimality.

Language: write the entire proof in English.

proof:
**Theorem.** There is no rational number whose square is 2.

---

### Setting up: from a rational square root to a whole-number equation

Suppose, for contradiction, that some rational number $r$ satisfies $r^2 = 2$. Since $(-r)^2 = r^2$, we may replace $r$ by $-r$ if necessary and assume $r > 0$. Being a positive rational, $r$ can be written as a ratio of two positive integers,
$$r = \frac{p}{q}, \qquad p, q \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}.$$
Clearing denominators in $r^2 = 2$ gives
$$p^2 = 2q^2. \tag{$\ast$}$$

So the whole assumption "$\sqrt 2$ is rational" is equivalent to the assertion that the equation $p^2 = 2q^2$ has a solution in positive integers. Our task is to show that it does not. Notice that we have deliberately *not* assumed that $p/q$ is in lowest terms; the classical parity proof uses that, but we will not need it. Instead we will use a different, and in some ways more vivid, form of minimality.

**The minimality choice.** Consider the set
$$S = \{\, p \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} : p^2 = 2q^2 \text{ for some } q \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \,\}.$$
By the paragraph above, our assumption says that $S$ is nonempty. Since $S$ is a nonempty set of positive integers, the well-ordering principle guarantees that $S$ has a least element. Fix such a least element $p$, and fix a positive integer $q$ with
$$p^2 = 2q^2 .$$
Our goal is now to manufacture, out of this pair $(p,q)$, a *strictly smaller* solution — a pair $(p', q')$ of positive integers with $p'^2 = 2q'^2$ and $p' < p$. That will contradict the minimality of $p$ and finish the proof.

The whole point of the argument that follows is that the manufacturing can be *seen*, not merely computed.

---

### Reading the equation as a statement about areas

Here is the idea. The equation $p^2 = 2q^2$ says:

> A square of side $p$ has exactly the same area as two squares of side $q$ put together.

That is a geometric statement about actual squares in the plane, and geometry offers a natural thing to do with it: *try to fit the two small squares inside the big one.* Of course they cannot fit without overlapping, since together they have exactly the big square's area and they certainly cannot tile it (two squares can never be cut-free arranged to fill a larger square). So when we place them inside, they must overlap somewhere and must leave something uncovered — and the areas of "overlap" and "leftover" must be equal, because the total area available is exactly the total area of the two squares. The miracle of Tennenbaum's argument is that if we place the two squares in *opposite corners*, then both the overlap and the leftover are again squares with whole-number sides, and the resulting equation "one square $=$ two squares" is a strictly smaller instance of the same equation. This is descent made visible.

**First, two inequalities that make the picture possible.** We need to know that each small square fits inside the big one, and that when pushed into opposite corners they genuinely overlap.

*Claim: $q < p < 2q$.*

Indeed, $p^2 = 2q^2 > q^2$, and since $p,q > 0$ this gives $p > q$. Also $p^2 = 2q^2 < 4q^2 = (2q)^2$, and again since $p, 2q > 0$ this gives $p < 2q$. (Both inequalities are strict; note in particular that $p = 2q$ is impossible, since it would force $4q^2 = 2q^2$, i.e. $q = 0$.)

Consequently the two integers
$$p' := 2q - p, \qquad q' := p - q$$
are both **strictly positive**. These will be the sides of the overlap square and of the leftover squares, respectively. Let us now see that geometrically.

---

### The picture

Work in the coordinate plane. Let the big square be
$$B = [0,p] \times [0,p], \qquad \text{area } p^2 .$$
Place one square of side $q$ in the bottom-left corner and one in the top-right corner:
$$A_1 = [0,q] \times [0,q], \qquad A_2 = [p-q,\,p] \times [p-q,\,p].$$
Because $q < p$, each $A_i$ is genuinely contained in $B$. Because $p < 2q$, i.e. $p - q < q$, the two squares overlap: the interval $[p-q, q]$ is nondegenerate.

**The doubly covered region.** A point $(x,y)$ lies in both $A_1$ and $A_2$ exactly when $p - q \le x \le q$ and $p-q \le y \le q$. So
$$A_1 \cap A_2 = [p-q,\,q] \times [p-q,\,q],$$
a square whose side is
$$q - (p - q) = 2q - p = p' > 0, \qquad \text{area } (2q-p)^2 .$$
This is the little square sitting in the middle of the picture, covered twice.

**The uncovered region.** I claim that the part of $B$ not covered by $A_1 \cup A_2$ consists of two squares of side $p - q$, namely the bottom-right and top-left corner squares
$$C_1 = [q,\,p] \times [0,\,p-q], \qquad C_2 = [0,\,p-q] \times [q,\,p],$$
each of side length $p - q = q' > 0$, hence each of area $(p-q)^2$. (They are disjoint apart from nothing at all: the first has $x \ge q > p-q$ while the second has $x \le p-q$.)

Let us verify the claim honestly, since the whole proof rests on it. Take $(x,y) \in B$, so $0 \le x,y \le p$.

*Every point of $C_1$ and of $C_2$ is uncovered.* If $(x,y) \in C_1$ then $x \ge q$, and in fact $x > q$ unless $x=q$; more usefully, $y \le p - q < q \le x$. Since $x \ge q$, the point can only fail to be in $A_1$ if $x > q$ — so let us instead argue with the interiors, which is all that matters for area, or better, argue directly: $(x,y) \in A_1$ requires $x \le q$ and $(x,y) \in A_2$ requires $y \ge p-q$. On $C_1$ we have $x \ge q$ and $y \le p-q$, so a point of $C_1$ lies in $A_1 \cup A_2$ only if $x = q$ or $y = p-q$, i.e. only on the boundary of $C_1$. The same argument applies to $C_2$ by symmetry (interchange the roles of $x$ and $y$). Thus the interiors of $C_1$ and $C_2$ are disjoint from $A_1 \cup A_2$.

*Every uncovered point lies in $C_1 \cup C_2$.* Suppose $(x,y) \in B$ lies in neither $A_1$ nor $A_2$. Since $(x,y) \notin A_1$, either $x > q$ or $y > q$. Since $(x,y) \notin A_2$, either $x < p - q$ or $y < p-q$. Suppose first $x > q$. As $q \ge p - q$ (because $p \le 2q$), we get $x > p-q$, so the second alternative must be realized by $y$: $y < p - q$. Then $q \le x \le p$ and $0 \le y \le p-q$, i.e. $(x,y) \in C_1$. In the remaining case $y > q$, the symmetric argument gives $x < p-q$ and hence $(x,y) \in C_2$.

So, up to boundary segments (which have zero area and therefore do not affect any of the computations below), the big square $B$ is decomposed as
$$B = \underbrace{(A_1 \cup A_2)}_{\text{covered}} \ \cup \ \underbrace{C_1 \cup C_2}_{\text{uncovered}} .$$

---

### Comparing the areas: overlap $=$ leftover

Now we simply count area two ways. Since $A_1 \cup A_2$ and $C_1 \cup C_2$ together make up $B$, and overlap only in boundary,
$$\operatorname{area}(A_1 \cup A_2) + \operatorname{area}(C_1) + \operatorname{area}(C_2) = \operatorname{area}(B) = p^2 .$$
On the other hand, by inclusion–exclusion (add the two squares' areas, then subtract the part counted twice),
$$\operatorname{area}(A_1 \cup A_2) = \operatorname{area}(A_1) + \operatorname{area}(A_2) - \operatorname{area}(A_1 \cap A_2) = q^2 + q^2 - (2q-p)^2 .$$
Substituting, and using $\operatorname{area}(C_1) = \operatorname{area}(C_2) = (p-q)^2$:
$$2q^2 - (2q-p)^2 + 2(p-q)^2 = p^2 .$$
But now comes the crucial input: by hypothesis $p^2 = 2q^2$, so the terms $2q^2$ and $p^2$ cancel, leaving exactly
$$\boxed{(2q-p)^2 = 2\,(p-q)^2 .}$$

In words: **the doubly covered middle square has the same area as the two uncovered corner squares together.** This is precisely the "one square equals two squares" relation we started with — but for smaller squares.

(For the reader who wants to see the identity without any appeal to area, here is the same computation done blind: using $4q^2 = 2p^2$,
$$(2q-p)^2 = 4q^2 - 4pq + p^2 = 2p^2 - 4pq + p^2 = 3p^2 - 4pq,$$
$$2(p-q)^2 = 2p^2 - 4pq + 2q^2 = 2p^2 - 4pq + p^2 = 3p^2 - 4pq.$$
They agree. But the point of Tennenbaum's argument is that this coincidence is not a coincidence: it is the visible fact that in our picture "counted twice" and "not counted at all" must balance.)

---

### The descent, and the contradiction

Set
$$p' = 2q - p, \qquad q' = p - q .$$
We have established three things:

1. $p'$ and $q'$ are integers — obvious, since $p$ and $q$ are.
2. $p' > 0$ and $q' > 0$ — this was the claim $q < p < 2q$ proved above; geometrically, $p' > 0$ says the two small squares really do overlap, and $q' > 0$ says they really do leave corners uncovered.
3. $p'^2 = 2q'^2$ — the boxed area identity.

Hence $p' \in S$. But
$$p' = 2q - p < 2p - p = p,$$
using $q < p$. (Geometrically: the middle overlap square is strictly smaller than the big square — indeed it is strictly inside it.) So $p'$ is an element of $S$ strictly smaller than $p$.

This contradicts the choice of $p$ as the *least* element of $S$.

Therefore $S$ is empty: there are no positive integers $p, q$ with $p^2 = 2q^2$. Consequently there is no positive rational $p/q$ whose square is $2$, and hence — since squaring is unaffected by sign, and $0^2 = 0 \ne 2$ — no rational number at all whose square is $2$. $\blacksquare$

---

### A remark on what the argument really shows

It is worth pausing over why this proof feels different from the usual parity argument. The usual proof says: a solution in lowest terms leads to $p$ and $q$ both even, which is absurd. Tennenbaum's proof never mentions even and odd, and never mentions lowest terms. Instead it takes *any* solution and physically produces a smaller one: draw a $p \times p$ square, shove the two $q \times q$ squares into opposite corners, and read off the new solution from the picture — the new "big square" is the doubly covered middle square, of side $2q - p$, and the new "small squares" are the two uncovered corners, of side $p-q$. Since one cannot descend forever within the positive integers, no solution can exist at all. The same picture, run in reverse, is the geometry behind the classical approximations $\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{7}{5}, \tfrac{17}{12}, \dots$ to $\sqrt2$: the map $(p,q) \mapsto (2q-p,\,p-q)$ shrinks the ratio's "error", and its inverse $(p,q) \mapsto (p + 2q,\, p+q)$ generates ever better approximations — which come ever closer to $\sqrt 2$ but, as we have just proved, never reach it.

Proof technique (follow this approach and no other): The reciprocation argument of Conway and Guy: if the root is P/Q then it also equals 2/(the root) = 2Q/P, so P/Q and 2Q/P have the same fractional part; writing those parts as q/Q and p/P gives p/q equal to P/Q with p < P and q < Q, a strictly simpler representation. proof:
**Enunciado.** No existe ningún número racional cuyo cuadrado sea 2.

---

### 1. La idea del argumento, en palabras

Antes de escribir una sola fórmula conviene entender qué vamos a hacer, porque la demostración es una de las más bonitas y elementales que existen: no usa ninguna propiedad de la factorización de los enteros (nada de "todo entero se descompone en primos", nada de "si 2 divide a $P^2$ entonces 2 divide a $P$"). Sólo usa **una división con resto** y el hecho de que no se puede descender infinitamente entre los enteros positivos.

La observación clave —debida en esta forma a Conway y Guy— es la siguiente propiedad de reciprocidad del número $\sqrt 2$: si $x$ es un número positivo con $x^2=2$, entonces
$$x=\frac{2}{x}.$$
Es decir: $\sqrt 2$ *es igual a su propio "recíproco duplicado"*. Ahora bien, si además $x$ fuese racional, digamos $x=P/Q$ con $P,Q$ enteros positivos, esa igualdad dice que
$$\frac{P}{Q}=\frac{2Q}{P},$$
o sea que **la misma cantidad admite dos escrituras como fracción, una con denominador $Q$ y otra con denominador $P$**. Como veremos, $\sqrt2$ está estrictamente entre 1 y 2, de modo que ambas fracciones tienen parte entera 1 y por tanto la misma parte fraccionaria. La parte fraccionaria de $P/Q$ es un número de la forma $q/Q$ con $0<q<Q$ (aquí es donde entra la división con resto: $q$ es el resto de dividir $P$ por $Q$), y la parte fraccionaria de $2Q/P$ es un número de la forma $p/P$ con $0<p<P$. Igualando esas dos partes fraccionarias obtenemos
$$\frac{q}{Q}=\frac{p}{P}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{p}{q}=\frac{P}{Q}=x,$$
es decir: ¡una nueva escritura de $x$ como fracción con numerador **estrictamente menor** y denominador **estrictamente menor** que antes! Repitiendo el proceso obtendríamos denominadores positivos cada vez más pequeños, indefinidamente, lo cual es imposible. Ésa es toda la demostración. Pasemos ahora a los detalles con cuidado.

---

### 2. Reducción a fracciones de términos positivos

Supongamos, para llegar a una contradicción, que existe un número racional $r$ con $r^2=2$.

Primero, $r\neq 0$, porque $0^2=0\neq2$. Segundo, podemos suponer $r>0$: si $r<0$, entonces $-r>0$ es también racional y $(-r)^2=r^2=2$, así que sustituimos $r$ por $-r$.

Al ser $r$ racional y positivo, se puede escribir $r=P/Q$ con $P$ y $Q$ **enteros positivos** (si la escritura inicial tuviera numerador y denominador negativos, cambiamos el signo de ambos). Nótese que *no* suponemos que la fracción sea irreducible: eso sería usar factorización, y queremos evitarlo. Nos basta con:

> **Hipótesis (H).** El conjunto
> $$\mathcal{D}=\{\,Q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\ :\ \text{existe }P\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\text{ con }(P/Q)^2=2\,\}$$
> es no vacío.

Como $\mathcal D$ es un conjunto no vacío de enteros positivos, por el principio del buen orden posee un **mínimo**. Elijamos, pues, $Q$ el menor elemento de $\mathcal D$, y elijamos $P$ entero positivo con
$$\left(\frac{P}{Q}\right)^{2}=2,\qquad\text{es decir}\qquad P^{2}=2Q^{2}. \tag{1}$$
Toda la estrategia consistirá en fabricar, a partir de $P$ y $Q$, un elemento de $\mathcal D$ estrictamente menor que $Q$: eso contradirá la minimalidad y cerrará la prueba.

---

### 3. Localización: $1<P/Q<2$

Necesitamos saber entre qué enteros consecutivos vive nuestro número, porque vamos a hablar de partes enteras y fraccionarias. Escribamos $x=P/Q>0$, de modo que $x^2=2$.

* Si fuese $x\le 1$, entonces, al ser $x>0$, multiplicando la desigualdad $x\le 1$ por sí misma se obtiene $x^2\le 1<2$, contradicción.
* Si fuese $x\ge 2$, entonces igualmente $x^2\ge 4>2$, contradicción.

Por tanto
$$1<x=\frac{P}{Q}<2. \tag{2}$$
Multiplicando por $Q>0$:
$$Q<P<2Q. \tag{3}$$

Obsérvese que esto ya nos dice que la parte entera de $x$ es $1$; el "verdadero contenido" de $x$ está en su parte fraccionaria, y es ahí donde vamos a mirar.

---

### 4. La reciprocidad: $x$ tiene una segunda escritura

De $x^2=2$ y $x\neq0$ se sigue, dividiendo por $x$,
$$x=\frac{2}{x}=\frac{2}{P/Q}=\frac{2Q}{P}. \tag{4}$$
Esto es la reciprocidad prometida: el mismo número $x$ se escribe con denominador $Q$ y numerador $P$, y también con denominador $P$ y numerador $2Q$. (Que $2Q/P$ es una fracción de enteros positivos es claro.) Combinando (4) con (2):
$$1<\frac{2Q}{P}<2,\qquad\text{es decir}\qquad P<2Q<2P. \tag{5}$$

---

### 5. Un solo paso de división con resto

Aquí es donde usamos, literalmente una vez, la división euclídea; y nada más.

**Dividimos $P$ entre $Q$.** Por (3) tenemos $Q<P<2Q$, luego el cociente es $1$ y el resto es
$$q:=P-Q,\qquad\text{con}\qquad 0<q<Q. \tag{6}$$
(Las desigualdades son inmediatas de (3): $P>Q$ da $q>0$, y $P<2Q$ da $q<Q$.) En términos de partes enteras y fraccionarias, esto dice
$$\frac{P}{Q}=1+\frac{q}{Q},\qquad 0<\frac{q}{Q}<1. \tag{7}$$

**Dividimos $2Q$ entre $P$.** Por (5) tenemos $P<2Q<2P$, luego otra vez el cociente es $1$ y el resto es
$$p:=2Q-P,\qquad\text{con}\qquad 0<p<P, \tag{8}$$
y análogamente
$$\frac{2Q}{P}=1+\frac{p}{P},\qquad 0<\frac{p}{P}<1. \tag{9}$$

---

### 6. Igualar las partes fraccionarias

Por (4), los números de (7) y (9) son el mismo:
$$1+\frac{q}{Q}=x=1+\frac{p}{P}.$$
Restando 1 en ambos miembros:
$$\frac{q}{Q}=\frac{p}{P}. \tag{10}$$

(Si se prefiere el lenguaje de partes fraccionarias: dos números reales iguales tienen la misma parte entera y la misma parte fraccionaria, pues si $m+f=n+g$ con $m,n$ enteros y $0\le f,g<1$, entonces $m-n=g-f$ es un entero de valor absoluto menor que 1, luego $m=n$ y $f=g$. En nuestro caso ambas partes enteras son 1, y (10) es la igualdad de las partes fraccionarias.)

Vale la pena comprobar (10) también de manera directa, para ver que no hay ningún truco escondido: usando la relación $P^2=2Q^2$ de (1),
$$qP-pQ=(P-Q)P-(2Q-P)Q=P^{2}-PQ-2Q^{2}+PQ=P^{2}-2Q^{2}=0 .$$
Así que $qP=pQ$, que es exactamente (10).

---

### 7. La escritura más simple, y la contradicción

De (10), es decir de $qP=pQ$, y siendo $q>0$ y $Q>0$, obtenemos
$$\frac{p}{q}=\frac{P}{Q}=x .$$
(En efecto: de $qP=pQ$ se sigue $\dfrac{p}{q}=\dfrac{P}{Q}$ dividiendo ambos lados por $qQ>0$.)

Por consiguiente $p$ y $q$ son **enteros positivos** —por (6) y (8)— con
$$\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)^{2}=x^{2}=2,$$
de modo que $q\in\mathcal D$. Pero (6) dice que
$$q<Q,$$
lo cual contradice que $Q$ fuera el **mínimo** de $\mathcal D$.

(Y de paso, obsérvese también $p<P$ por (8): la nueva fracción es más simple en ambos términos. Si en lugar de invocar el buen orden preferimos el lenguaje del descenso infinito, el argumento se lee así: de cualquier representación $P/Q$ de $\sqrt 2$ con enteros positivos fabricamos otra, $p/q$, con $0<q<Q$; iterando, obtendríamos una sucesión infinita y estrictamente decreciente $Q>q>\dots$ de enteros positivos, lo cual es imposible.)

---

### 8. Conclusión

El número $\sqrt2$ satisface $x=2/x$; escrito con una fracción, esto obliga a que $P/Q$ y $2Q/P$ sean el mismo número. Dos fracciones iguales con distinto denominador no son en sí mismas contradictorias, claro; lo decisivo es que al comparar sus **partes fraccionarias** —que es lo mismo que hacer una división con resto en cada una— los papeles de $P$ y $Q$ se intercambian, y los restos son necesariamente *más pequeños* que los divisores. Como entre los enteros positivos no se puede descender para siempre, ninguna representación fraccionaria puede existir. **Theorem.** There is no $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $r^{2}=2$.

Throughout, we freely invoke the following named results.

* **(G)** *Gauss's irreducibility theorem for cyclotomic polynomials*: for every $n\ge 1$ the $n$-th cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_n$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[X]$; consequently, if $\zeta_n$ is a primitive $n$-th root of unity, then $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois of degree $\varphi(n)$ and the *cyclotomic character*
$$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}),\qquad a\longmapsto \sigma_a,\quad \sigma_a(\zeta_n)=\zeta_n^{a},$$
is a group isomorphism.
* **(FTGT)** The *Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory*: for a finite Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ with group $G$, the maps $H\mapsto K^{H}$ and $L\mapsto \operatorname{Gal}(K/L)$ are mutually inverse, inclusion-reversing bijections between subgroups of $G$ and intermediate fields, and $[K^{H}:\mathbb{Q}]=[G:H]$.
* **(KD)** *Dedekind's factorization theorem* (Kummer–Dedekind): let $L=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$ with $\theta$ an algebraic integer of minimal polynomial $g\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$, let $\mathcal{O}_L$ be the ring of integers of $L$, and let $p$ be a prime with $p\nmid[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\theta]]$. Then the factorization type of $p\mathcal{O}_L$ into prime ideals of $\mathcal{O}_L$ is the mirror image of the factorization of $g$ in $\mathbb{F}_p[X]$: the primes above $p$ correspond to the monic irreducible factors of $g \bmod p$, with matching residue degrees and exponents. We also use *Dedekind's discriminant–index formula* $\operatorname{disc}(g)=[\mathcal{O}_L:\mathbb{Z}[\theta]]^{2}\,d_L$.
* **(AR)** *Artin reciprocity in the cyclotomic case* (Frobenius' law for $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$): if $p\nmid n$ is prime, then $p$ is unramified in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ and its Frobenius automorphism is $\operatorname{Frob}_p=\sigma_{p \bmod n}$ under the isomorphism of **(G)**. Moreover Frobenius elements are functorial: for an intermediate field $L$, the Frobenius at the prime of $L$ below a chosen prime of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ is $\operatorname{Frob}_p|_{L}$, and for $L/\mathbb{Q}$ Galois the residue degree of $p$ in $L$ equals the order of $\operatorname{Frob}_p|_L$ in $\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$.
* **(Ch)** The *Chebotarev density theorem*: if $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is finite Galois with group $G$ and $C\subseteq G$ is a conjugacy class, then the set of primes $p$, unramified in $K$, with $\operatorname{Frob}_p\in C$ has natural density $|C|/|G|$; in particular this set is infinite. (For $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ this specializes, via **(AR)**, to *Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions*.)

---

### Step 1. The cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_8)$ and the element $\tau$

Let $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/8}$, a primitive $8$-th root of unity, and let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$. Since $\Phi_8(X)=X^{4}+1$, theorem **(G)** gives that $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois of degree $\varphi(8)=4$ with
$$G:=\operatorname{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})=\{\sigma_1,\sigma_3,\sigma_5,\sigma_7\}\;\cong\;(\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z})^{\times},\qquad \sigma_a(\zeta)=\zeta^{a}.$$

Put
$$\tau:=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}\in K .$$
Since $\zeta^{4}=-1$, we have $\zeta^{-2}=-\zeta^{2}$, hence
$$\tau^{2}=\zeta^{2}+2+\zeta^{-2}=2. \tag{1}$$
In particular $\tau\neq 0$. Note also that $\tau$ is an algebraic integer, being a sum of roots of unity.

From $\zeta^{4}=-1$ we get $\zeta^{3}=-\zeta^{-1}$ and $\zeta^{5}=-\zeta$, so
$$\sigma_7(\tau)=\zeta^{7}+\zeta^{-7}=\zeta^{-1}+\zeta=\tau,\qquad
\sigma_3(\tau)=\zeta^{3}+\zeta^{-3}=-\zeta^{-1}-\zeta=-\tau,\qquad
\sigma_5(\tau)=-\tau. \tag{2}$$

Thus $H:=\{\sigma_1,\sigma_7\}$ is a subgroup of $G$ of index $2$ fixing $\tau$. By **(FTGT)**, $F:=K^{H}$ satisfies $[F:\mathbb{Q}]=[G:H]=2$, and $\tau\in F$. Since $\sigma_3\in G\setminus H$ satisfies $\sigma_3(\tau)=-\tau\neq\tau$ (as $\tau\ne0$), the element $\tau$ is not fixed by all of $G$, so $\tau\notin\mathbb{Q}=K^{G}$. Hence $\mathbb{Q}\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}(\tau)\subseteq F$ and $[F:\mathbb{Q}]=2$ force
$$F=\mathbb{Q}(\tau),\qquad [\mathbb{Q}(\tau):\mathbb{Q}]=2,$$
and by (1) the minimal polynomial of $\tau$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is $g(X)=X^{2}-2$. In particular $F/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois with group $\operatorname{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})=G/H=\{\mathrm{id},\ \sigma_3|_F\}$, and $\sigma_3|_F\ne \mathrm{id}$.

### Step 2. For every prime $p\equiv 3 \pmod 8$, the class of $2$ is not a square in $\mathbb{F}_p$

Let $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$; in particular $p$ is odd, so $p\nmid 8$ and by **(AR)** $p$ is unramified in $K$ with $\operatorname{Frob}_p=\sigma_{p\bmod 8}=\sigma_3$. By the functoriality statement in **(AR)**, the Frobenius of $p$ in $\operatorname{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ is $\sigma_3|_{F}$, which by Step 1 is nontrivial, hence of order $2$. Therefore the residue degree of $p$ in $F$ equals $2$: the prime $p$ is inert in $\mathcal{O}_F$, i.e. $p\mathcal{O}_F$ is a prime ideal with residue field $\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}$.

Now apply **(KD)** with $\theta=\tau$, $g(X)=X^{2}-2$, $L=F$. We have $\operatorname{disc}(g)=8$, so by Dedekind's discriminant–index formula $[\mathcal{O}_F:\mathbb{Z}[\tau]]^{2}$ divides $8$, whence $[\mathcal{O}_F:\mathbb{Z}[\tau]]\in\{1,2\}$ and, $p$ being odd, $p\nmid[\mathcal{O}_F:\mathbb{Z}[\tau]]$. Thus **(KD)** applies and tells us that the factorization type of $p\mathcal{O}_F$ mirrors that of $X^{2}-2$ in $\mathbb{F}_p[X]$. Since $p$ is inert (one prime above $p$, of residue degree $2$), the polynomial $X^{2}-2$ must be **irreducible** in $\mathbb{F}_p[X]$. Equivalently:
$$\text{there is no }u\in\mathbb{F}_p\text{ with }u^{2}=\bar 2. \tag{3}$$
(This is precisely the second supplementary law of quadratic reciprocity, $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=(-1)^{(p^{2}-1)/8}=-1$ for $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$, here obtained from cyclotomic class field theory.)

### Step 3. Existence of suitable primes

By **(Ch)** applied to $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_8)$ and the conjugacy class $\{\sigma_3\}$ of the abelian group $G$ (all classes are singletons), the set
$$S=\{p \text{ prime}:\ \operatorname{Frob}_p=\sigma_3\}$$
has density $1/4$; by **(AR)** this is exactly the set of primes $p\equiv 3\pmod 8$. Being of positive density, $S$ is infinite. (This is Dirichlet's theorem for the progression $3\bmod 8$.)

### Step 4. Conclusion

Suppose, for contradiction, that $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ satisfies $r^{2}=2$. Write $r=a/b$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$, $b\neq 0$, so that
$$a^{2}=2b^{2}. \tag{4}$$
Since $S$ is infinite by Step 3 while $b$ has only finitely many prime divisors, we may choose a prime $p\in S$ (so $p\equiv 3 \pmod 8$) with $p\nmid b$. Reducing (4) modulo $p$ and writing $\bar{\cdot}$ for classes in $\mathbb{F}_p$, we have $\bar b\neq 0$, hence $\bar b$ is invertible in the field $\mathbb{F}_p$, and
$$\bigl(\bar a\,\bar b^{-1}\bigr)^{2}=\bar a^{2}\bar b^{-2}=\overline{2b^{2}}\,\bar b^{-2}=\bar 2 .$$
So $\bar 2$ is a square in $\mathbb{F}_p$, contradicting (3).

Therefore no rational number has square $2$. $\blacksquare$

*(Remark: Step 1 already exhibits the contradiction in a second way: if $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ had $r^2=2$, then $X^{2}-2=(X-r)(X+r)$ in $\mathbb{Q}[X]\subseteq K[X]$, so the root $\tau$ of $X^2-2$ in $K$ would equal $\pm r\in\mathbb{Q}$; but every element of $\mathbb{Q}$ is fixed by $\sigma_3$, whereas $\sigma_3(\tau)=-\tau$ by (2), forcing $\tau=0$ and hence $2=\tau^{2}=0$, absurd. Equivalently, by the Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory $[\mathbb{Q}(\tau):\mathbb{Q}]=2\ne 1$.)*

**定理** 平方が 6 に等しい有理数は存在しない。

**準備（補題）** 整数 $n$ について，$n^2$ が偶数ならば $n$ は偶数である。

*証明* 対偶を示す。$n$ が奇数ならば，ある整数 $k$ を用いて $n=2k+1$ と書ける。このとき
$$n^2=(2k+1)^2=4k^2+4k+1=2(2k^2+2k)+1$$
であり，$2k^2+2k$ は整数だから $n^2$ は奇数である。よって $n^2$ が偶数ならば $n$ は偶数である。∎

**定理の証明** 結論を否定し，$r^2=6$ を満たす有理数 $r$ が存在すると仮定する。

$(-r)^2=r^2=6$ であり，また $0^2=0\neq 6$ だから，$r\neq 0$ であり，$r$ か $-r$ の一方は正である。したがって最初から $r>0$ と仮定してよい。

$r$ は正の有理数だから，$r=\dfrac{p}{q}$（$p,q$ は正の整数）と表せる。ここで，そのような表し方すべてを考え，分母 $q$ が最小となるものを選ぶ（正の整数の空でない集合には最小元が存在するので，このような選択が可能である）。この選び方のもとでは $p,q$ は共通の素因数を持たない，特に $p$ と $q$ が共に偶数であることはない。実際，$p=2p'$，$q=2q'$（$p',q'$ は正の整数）と書けたとすれば $r=\dfrac{p'}{q'}$ となり，$q'=q/2<q$ が $q$ の最小性に反する。

さて $r^2=6$ より $\dfrac{p^2}{q^2}=6$，すなわち
$$p^2=6q^2 \qquad \cdots (1)$$
が成り立つ。

$(1)$ の右辺 $6q^2=2\cdot 3q^2$ は偶数だから $p^2$ は偶数であり，補題より $p$ は偶数である。よって $p=2m$（$m$ は正の整数）と書ける。これを $(1)$ に代入すると
$$4m^2=6q^2,$$
両辺を $2$ で割って
$$2m^2=3q^2 \qquad \cdots (2)$$
を得る。

$(2)$ の左辺 $2m^2$ は偶数だから，$3q^2$ は偶数である。また $4q^2=2\cdot 2q^2$ は偶数である。したがって
$$q^2=4q^2-3q^2$$
は（偶数）$-$（偶数）であるから偶数である。ふたたび補題より $q$ は偶数である。

こうして $p$ と $q$ が共に偶数となったが，これは $p,q$ の選び方（$p$ と $q$ が共に偶数にはならないこと）に矛盾する。

ゆえに $r^2=6$ を満たす有理数 $r$ は存在しない。∎

---

### 補題 1（除法の原理）

$a\in\mathbb{Z}$, $b\in\mathbb{Z}$, $b>0$ とする。このとき $a=bk+r$, $0\le r<b$ となる整数 $k,r$ が存在する。

**証明** 集合
$$S=\{\,a-bk \;:\; k\in\mathbb{Z},\ a-bk\ge 0\,\}$$
を考える。$k=-|a|$ とすると、$b\ge 1$ より $a-bk=a+b|a|\ge a+|a|\ge 0$ であるから $S\neq\varnothing$。$S$ は非負整数の空でない集合だから、自然数の整列性により最小元 $r=a-bk$ が存在する。もし $r\ge b$ なら $r-b=a-b(k+1)\ge 0$ より $r-b\in S$ であり、$r-b<r$（$b>0$）は $r$ の最小性に反する。ゆえに $0\le r<b$。$\blacksquare$

### 補題 2（ベズーの等式）

$p,q$ を整数とし、$p,q$ の正の公約数が $1$ のみであるとする（このとき $p,q$ は互いに素という）。ただし $q>0$ とする。このとき整数 $a,b$ が存在して
$$ap+bq=1 .$$

**証明** 集合
$$I=\{\,ap+bq \;:\; a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\,\},\qquad I^{+}=\{\,x\in I \;:\; x>0\,\}$$
を考える。$q=0\cdot p+1\cdot q>0$ より $I^{+}\neq\varnothing$。整列性により $I^{+}$ の最小元 $d=a_0p+b_0q>0$ が存在する。

$d$ が $p$ を割ることを示す。補題 1 より $p=dk+r$, $0\le r<d$ と書ける。すると
$$r=p-dk=(1-a_0k)p+(-b_0k)q\in I .$$
$r>0$ ならば $r\in I^{+}$ かつ $r<d$ となり $d$ の最小性に反する。よって $r=0$、すなわち $d\mid p$。同様に（$q=dk'+r'$ として）$d\mid q$。

したがって $d$ は $p,q$ の正の公約数であり、仮定より $d=1$。ゆえに $a_0p+b_0q=1$。$\blacksquare$

### 補題 3

$p,q$ が互いに素（$q>0$）で $n\ge 1$ が整数ならば、$p^n$ と $q$ も互いに素である。

**証明** 補題 2 により $ap+bq=1$ となる整数 $a,b$ をとる。両辺を $n$ 乗し、二項定理で展開すると
$$1=(ap+bq)^n=(ap)^n+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\binom{n}{j}(ap)^{n-j}(bq)^{j}
=a^n p^n+q\cdot B,$$
ここで $B=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\binom{n}{j}a^{n-j}p^{n-j}b^{j}q^{j-1}$ は整数である（各項は $j\ge1$ より $q$ を少なくとも 1 個含む）。よって整数 $A=a^n,\;B$ により
$$A\,p^n+B\,q=1 .$$
$p^n$ と $q$ の任意の公約数 $e$ はこの左辺を割るので $e\mid 1$、すなわち $e=\pm1$。ゆえに正の公約数は $1$ のみ。$\blacksquare$

### 命題（有理根定理・モニックの場合）

$n\ge 1$、$c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{n-1}\in\mathbb{Z}$ とし、
$$f(x)=x^{n}+c_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1x+c_0$$
とおく。有理数 $r$ が $f(r)=0$ を満たすならば、$r$ は整数である。

**証明** $r$ は有理数だから、$r=p/q$（$p\in\mathbb{Z}$, $q\in\mathbb{Z}$, $q>0$）と書ける。そのような表示のうち分母 $q$ が最小のものをとる（整列性）。このとき $p,q$ は互いに素である。実際、$d>1$ が $p,q$ の公約数なら $p'=p/d,\;q'=q/d$ は整数で $q'>0$, $r=p'/q'$ かつ $q'<q$ となり、$q$ の最小性に反する。

$f(p/q)=0$ の両辺に $q^{n}$ を掛けると
$$p^{n}+c_{n-1}p^{n-1}q+c_{n-2}p^{n-2}q^{2}+\cdots+c_0q^{n}=0,$$
すなわち
$$p^{n}=-q\bigl(c_{n-1}p^{n-1}+c_{n-2}p^{n-2}q+\cdots+c_0q^{n-1}\bigr).$$
右辺の括弧内は整数だから、$q\mid p^{n}$。一方、補題 3 より $p^n$ と $q$ は互いに素であり、$q$ は $p^n$ と $q$ の正の公約数であるから $q=1$。ゆえに $r=p\in\mathbb{Z}$。$\blacksquare$

### 定理の証明

$f(x)=x^{2}-2$ はモニックな整数係数多項式である。もし有理数 $r$ が $r^{2}=2$ を満たすとすると $f(r)=0$ であるから、上の命題より $r$ は整数である。そこで整数 $m$ で $m^{2}=2$ となるものがあるとして矛盾を導く。

- $|m|\le 1$ のとき：$m^{2}=|m|^{2}\le 1<2$。
- $|m|\ge 2$ のとき：$m^{2}=|m|^{2}\ge 4>2$。

整数 $m$ は必ずこのいずれかを満たすので、いずれの場合も $m^{2}\neq 2$ となり矛盾。

したがって、平方が $2$ に等しい有理数は存在しない。$\blacksquare$

$(x,y)\in S$ とする。$(x,y)\notin A \iff (x>q \ \text{または}\ y>q)$、$(x,y)\notin B \iff (x<p-q\ \text{または}\ y<p-q)$。(1) より $p-q<q$ なので $x>q$ かつ $x<p-q$ は不可能、$y>q$ かつ $y<p-q$ も不可能。ゆえに

$$\mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)-\mu(A\cap B)=2q^{2}-(2q-p)^{2}=p^{2}-(2q-p)^{2},$$

$$\mu\bigl(S\setminus(A\cup B)\bigr)=p^{2}-\mu(A\cup B)=(2q-p)^{2}.$$
一方 (3) より $\mu\bigl(S\setminus(A\cup B)\bigr)=2(p-q)^{2}$。したがって

proof:
**定理.** 有理数 $r$ で $r^2=2$ となるものは存在しない。

**証明の着想（どこから来ているか）.**
通常の証明は「偶奇」や素因数分解という整数論の内側の道具を使う。ここでは代わりに、**実数直線の加法群の部分群に関する位相・力学系的な原理**を用いる：

> 「$\mathbb{R}$ の非自明な *離散* 部分群は、縮小写像（$0<\lambda<1$ による掛け算）で自分自身の中に写されることはない。」

一方、$\sqrt2$ が有理数だとすると $\mathbb{Z}+\mathbb{Z}\sqrt2$ は $\frac1q\mathbb{Z}$ の中に入るので離散群になる。ところが $\lambda=\sqrt2-1$ は $0<\lambda<1$ を満たす**この群の元**であり、群が乗法で閉じているために縮小写像 $x\mapsto \lambda x$ がこの群を保つ。これが矛盾を生む。整数の素因数分解は一度も使わない。

---

### 準備となる補題

**補題 1（ベルヌーイの不等式）.** $h>0$ と任意の自然数 $n\ge 1$ に対し $(1+h)^n\ge 1+nh$。

*証明.* $n$ についての帰納法。$n=1$ では等号。$(1+h)^{n}\ge 1+nh$ を仮定すると
$$(1+h)^{n+1}=(1+h)^n(1+h)\ \ge\ (1+nh)(1+h)=1+(n+1)h+nh^2\ \ge\ 1+(n+1)h .\qquad\square$$

**系 2.** $0<\lambda<1$ かつ $\delta>0$ ならば、ある自然数 $n$ に対して $\lambda^n<\delta$ となる。

*証明.* $h:=\frac1\lambda-1>0$ とおくと $\frac1\lambda=1+h$ である。補題 1 より
$$\frac{1}{\lambda^{n}}=(1+h)^n\ \ge\ 1+nh .$$
よって $\lambda^n\le \frac{1}{1+nh}$。$h>0$ だから $n>\frac{1}{h\delta}$ となる自然数 $n$ を取れば $1+nh>\frac1\delta$、したがって $\lambda^n<\delta$。$\square$

**補題 3（縮小原理）.** $G\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ を加法について閉じた集合（部分群）とし、次を仮定する：

1. $G$ は $0$ でない元 $x_0$ を含む；
2. ある $\delta>0$ があって、$G$ の任意の元 $x\neq 0$ は $|x|\ge\delta$ を満たす（**離散性**）；
3. ある実数 $\lambda$ が $0<\lambda<1$ と $\lambda G\subseteq G$ を満たす（**縮小性**）。

このとき矛盾が生じる。すなわち 1., 2., 3. を同時に満たす $G,\lambda$ は存在しない。

*証明.* 条件 3 を繰り返し使うと、すべての $n\ge 0$ に対し $\lambda^n x_0\in G$ である（$n$ についての帰納法：$\lambda^{n+1}x_0=\lambda(\lambda^n x_0)\in \lambda G\subseteq G$）。$\lambda>0$、$x_0\neq0$ より $\lambda^n x_0\neq 0$ であるから、条件 2 より
$$\lambda^{n}|x_0|\ \ge\ \delta\qquad(\forall n\ge 0),$$
すなわち $\lambda^n\ge \delta/|x_0|>0$ が全ての $n$ で成り立つ。しかし系 2 を $\delta/|x_0|>0$ に適用すると、ある $n$ で $\lambda^n<\delta/|x_0|$ となり、矛盾。$\square$

---

### 定理の証明

$r^2=2$ を満たす有理数 $r$ が存在したと仮定する。$0^2=0\neq2$ だから $r\neq0$ であり、$(-r)^2=r^2$ なので、はじめから $r>0$ としてよい。$r$ は正の有理数なので、正の整数 $p,q$ を用いて
$$r=\frac{p}{q}$$
と書ける。

**（i）$1<r<2$ であること.** もし $r\le 1$ なら $0<r\le1$ より $r^2\le r\le 1<2$ となり矛盾。もし $r\ge2$ なら $r^2\ge 2r\ge 4>2$ となり矛盾。よって $1<r<2$。

**（ii）集合 $G$ の定義とその性質.**
$$G:=\{\,a+br\ :\ a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\,\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$$
とおく。

*加法について閉じている：* $(a+br)-(c+dr)=(a-c)+(b-d)r\in G$。特に $G$ は $\mathbb{R}$ の部分群である。

*乗法についても閉じている：* ここで $r^2=2$ を使う。
$$(a+br)(c+dr)=ac+(ad+bc)r+bd\,r^{2}=(ac+2bd)+(ad+bc)r\in G .$$

*$0$ でない元を含む：* $1=1+0\cdot r\in G$、$1\neq0$。

*離散性：* $r=p/q$ だから、任意の $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ に対し
$$a+br=a+b\frac{p}{q}=\frac{aq+bp}{q}\in\frac1q\mathbb{Z},$$
すなわち $G\subseteq\frac1q\mathbb{Z}$。ゆえに $x\in G$、$x\neq0$ なら $x=\frac{m}{q}$（$m$ は $0$ でない整数）と書け、$|m|\ge1$ より
$$|x|\ \ge\ \frac1q\ >\ 0 .$$
つまり $\delta:=\frac1q$ が補題 3 の条件 2 を与える。

**（iii）縮小写像の存在.** $\lambda:=r-1$ とおく。（i）より $0<\lambda<1$。また $\lambda=-1+1\cdot r\in G$ であり、$G$ は乗法で閉じているから、任意の $g\in G$ に対して $\lambda g\in G$、すなわち
$$\lambda G\subseteq G .$$

**（iv）結論.** こうして $G$ と $\lambda$ は補題 3 の条件 1（$x_0=1$）、条件 2（$\delta=1/q$）、条件 3（$0<\lambda=r-1<1$）をすべて満たす。これは補題 3 に矛盾する。

したがって $r^2=2$ を満たす有理数 $r$ は存在しない。$\blacksquare$

---

**補足（矛盾の具体的な姿）.** 上の証明を展開すると、次の明示的な矛盾が得られる：$r=p/q$、$r^2=2$ なら、各 $n$ に対して $(r-1)^n$ は $a_n+b_nr$（$a_n,b_n\in\mathbb{Z}$）の形をもつので $q(r-1)^n$ は $0$ でない整数だが、$0<r-1<1$ より $n$ を大きくすれば $0<q(r-1)^n<1$ となる。$0$ と $1$ の間に整数はないので矛盾。すなわち、この証明の本質は「$\sqrt2-1$ が絶対値 $1$ より小さい**無限位数の単数**であり、縮小力学系を生む」という点にあり、素因数分解とはまったく別の方向から来ている。

proof:
设有理数 $r$ 满足 $r^2=2$。则 $r>0$，且 $r=\sqrt2$。置
$$S=\{\,q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\ :\ q\sqrt2\in\mathbb Z\,\}.$$
由 $r=m/n$（$m,n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$）得 $n\sqrt2=m\in\mathbb Z$，故 $n\in S$，$S\neq\varnothing$。由良序性，取 $q=\min S$，并置 $p=q\sqrt2\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$。于是
$$p^2=2q^2 .$$

**几何实现.** 取 $\triangle ABC$：$\angle B=90^\circ$，$AB=BC=q$。由勾股定理 $AC^2=2q^2=p^2$，故 $AC=p$。又 $\angle A=\angle C=45^\circ$。

**估界.** $p^2=2q^2>q^2\Rightarrow p>q$；$p=AC<AB+BC=2q$。故
$$q<p<2q. \tag{1}$$

**折叠.** 由 $(1)$ 有 $0<q<p$，故 $AC$ 上存在唯一点 $D$ 使 $AD=AB=q$，且 $D$ 内于 $AC$。设 $\ell$ 为过 $D$ 且垂直于 $AC$ 的直线；因 $\angle ADE'$ 与 $\angle C=45^\circ$ 之关系，$\ell$ 与线段 $BC$ 交于唯一点 $E$（$\ell$ 即将 $AC$ 折至 $AB$ 之折痕的垂足线：反射 $\sigma$ 沿 $AE$ 进行，见下）。

于 $\triangle ABE$ 与 $\triangle ADE$ 中：$\angle ABE=\angle ADE=90^\circ$，$AB=AD$，$AE$ 公共。故
$$\triangle ABE\cong\triangle ADE,\qquad BE=DE. \tag{2}$$
即沿直线 $AE$ 的反射把 $B\mapsto D$，把射线 $AB$ 映至射线 $AC$，把斜边贴合于直角边。

于 $\triangle CDE$ 中：$\angle CDE=90^\circ$，$\angle DCE=\angle C=45^\circ$，故 $\angle DEC=45^\circ$，从而
$$DE=DC. \tag{3}$$
且 $\triangle CDE$ 为等腰直角三角形，直角边 $DC=DE$，斜边 $CE$。

**计算.** 由 $(2),(3)$：
$$DC=AC-AD=p-q,\qquad DE=p-q,\qquad BE=p-q,$$
$$CE=BC-BE=q-(p-q)=2q-p.$$
由 $(1)$：$p-q>0$，$2q-p>0$，二者皆为正整数，且
$$p-q<q. \tag{4}$$

**下降.** $\triangle CDE$ 为等腰直角三角形，腰 $q'=p-q$，斜边 $p'=2q-p$，均属 $\mathbb Z_{>0}$。由勾股定理 $p'^2=2q'^2$，即
$$q'\sqrt2=p'\in\mathbb Z ,$$
（亦可直验：$(p-q)\sqrt2=p\sqrt2-q\sqrt2=2q-p$）。故 $q'\in S$。由 $(4)$，$0<q'<q=\min S$，矛盾。

故 $S=\varnothing$ 与假设不容，$\sqrt2$ 非有理数；即不存在有理数其平方为 $2$。$\blacksquare$

proof:
**Afirmación.** No existe ningún número racional $r$ tal que $r^2 = 17$.

**Demostración.** Supongamos, por reducción al absurdo, que existe un número racional $r$ con $r^2 = 17$.

*Paso 1: podemos suponer que $r$ es un cociente de enteros positivos.*

Como $0^2 = 0 \neq 17$, se tiene $r \neq 0$. Además $(-r)^2 = r^2 = 17$, de modo que, sustituyendo $r$ por $-r$ si fuera necesario, podemos suponer $r > 0$. Por ser racional, $r = m/n$ con $m, n$ enteros y $n \neq 0$; cambiando simultáneamente los signos de $m$ y $n$ si hace falta, podemos suponer $n > 0$, y entonces $m = rn > 0$. Así, $r$ se escribe como cociente de dos enteros positivos.

*Paso 2: elección de un denominador mínimo.*

Consideremos el conjunto
$$S = \{\, b \in \mathbb{Z} : b > 0 \ \text{y existe } a \in \mathbb{Z},\ a > 0,\ \text{con } r = a/b \,\}.$$
Por el Paso 1, $S \neq \varnothing$. Por el principio de buena ordenación de los enteros positivos, $S$ posee un elemento mínimo $b$. Sea $a$ un entero positivo con $r = a/b$.

De $r^2 = 17$ se obtiene $a^2/b^2 = 17$, es decir,
$$a^2 = 17\,b^2. \tag{1}$$

*Paso 3: acotación de $a$.*

Afirmamos que
$$4b < a \quad\text{y}\quad 4a < 17b. \tag{2}$$

En efecto, si fuera $a \le 4b$, como $a$ y $b$ son positivos se tendría $a^2 \le 16b^2 < 17b^2$, contradiciendo (1); luego $a > 4b$.

Análogamente, si fuera $4a \ge 17b$, entonces, siendo ambos miembros positivos, $16a^2 \ge 289\,b^2$; pero por (1) $16a^2 = 16\cdot 17\, b^2 = 272\,b^2 < 289\,b^2$, contradicción. Luego $4a < 17b$.

Observemos además que de $a^2 = 17b^2 < 25 b^2$ y de la positividad de $a$ y $5b$ se sigue
$$a < 5b, \tag{3}$$
pues si fuese $a \ge 5b$ tendríamos $a^2 \ge 25b^2 > 17b^2$.

*Paso 4: construcción de un denominador menor.*

Definamos
$$a' = 17b - 4a, \qquad b' = a - 4b.$$
Por (2), tanto $a'$ como $b'$ son enteros **positivos**. Además, por (3),
$$b' = a - 4b < 5b - 4b = b,$$
es decir, $0 < b' < b$.

Comprobemos que $a'/b' = r$. Usando (1):
$$a' \, b = (17b - 4a)b = 17b^2 - 4ab = a^2 - 4ab = a\,(a - 4b) = a\,b'.$$
Como $b > 0$ y $b' > 0$, dividiendo entre $b\,b'$ obtenemos
$$\frac{a'}{b'} = \frac{a}{b} = r.$$

*Paso 5: contradicción.*

Hemos hallado enteros positivos $a', b'$ con $r = a'/b'$ y $0 < b' < b$. Por tanto $b' \in S$ y $b' < b$, lo cual contradice la minimalidad de $b$ en $S$.

Esta contradicción proviene de suponer la existencia de un racional $r$ con $r^2 = 17$. Concluimos que ningún número racional tiene cuadrado igual a $17$. $\blacksquare$
